m7-t1.title: Association is not an intervention effect
m7-t1.summary: Correlation describes variables moving together; it does not identify which caused which or whether a third factor explains both.
m7-t1.explanation: Correlation describes variables moving together; it does not identify which caused which or whether a third factor explains both. Selection into training can differ from random assignment. Reverse causality is also possible: people intending to stay may be more likely to attend. Draw a simple causal sketch with the proposed intervention, outcome and plausible shared causes before recommending a causal statement.
m7-t1.example: Employees who attend an optional development workshop have lower turnover. A sponsor wants to claim the workshop caused retention. Participants may already be more motivated, have supportive managers or work different shifts. The association alone cannot separate these explanations.
m7-t1.takeaway: Recognise alternative explanations and design a more credible evaluation of an HR intervention.

m7-t1.title: Design comparison before launch
m7-t1.summary: Where ethical and practical, a randomised or phased rollout can improve the comparison, with appropriate consent, governance and no denial of essential support.
m7-t1.explanation: Where ethical and practical, a randomised or phased rollout can improve the comparison, with appropriate consent, governance and no denial of essential support. Where randomisation is not suitable, use a careful comparison group and document remaining differences. Collect a baseline and define the outcome window in advance. Do not choose the favourable metric after looking at results. Evaluation design should be proportionate to the decision.
m7-t1.example: Employees who attend an optional development workshop have lower turnover. A sponsor wants to claim the workshop caused retention. Participants may already be more motivated, have supportive managers or work different shifts. The association alone cannot separate these explanations.
m7-t1.takeaway: Recognise alternative explanations and design a more credible evaluation of an HR intervention.

m7-t1.title: Interpret uncertainty honestly
m7-t1.summary: Small samples, missing follow-up and changing conditions limit conclusions.
m7-t1.explanation: Small samples, missing follow-up and changing conditions limit conclusions. A before-and-after difference can be informative but is vulnerable to external changes. Report what was observed and what assumptions would be needed for a causal interpretation. Do not claim that a statistical adjustment automatically removes every bias. A sensible result can be “promising enough for a better-designed pilot”.
m7-t1.example: Before an onboarding change, a pilot group has 20% early exits and a comparison group 10%. Afterwards they have 12% and 8%. The pilot change is −8 percentage points and comparison change −2, giving a difference-in-differences estimate of −6 points. This illustrative estimate requires assumptions such as comparable underlying trends; the arithmetic alone does not prove causation.
m7-t1.takeaway: Recognise alternative explanations and design a more credible evaluation of an HR intervention.

m7-t2.title: Compare with a meaningful baseline
m7-t2.summary: Accuracy is correct predictions divided by all evaluated cases.
m7-t2.explanation: Accuracy is correct predictions divided by all evaluated cases. With imbalanced outcomes it can hide poor detection of the less common event. A confusion matrix separates true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. Precision asks how many positive predictions were correct; recall asks how many actual positives were detected. The positive class and evaluation period must be stated.
m7-t2.example: A vendor offers a model that is “90% accurate” at predicting exits. In the company’s synthetic sample, 90% of employees stay. A model that predicts everyone stays would also be 90% accurate while identifying no exits. The analyst must ask better questions.
m7-t2.takeaway: Interpret a simple classifier’s errors and identify why employee-risk predictions require strict governance.

m7-t2.title: Errors have different consequences
m7-t2.summary: A false positive may wrongly label someone likely to leave; a false negative misses an actual exit.
m7-t2.explanation: A false positive may wrongly label someone likely to leave; a false negative misses an actual exit. Neither error type should be reduced to a technical score without considering harm. Threshold changes trade off errors. A model score is not an explanation of a person’s intentions. This course reviews synthetic aggregate examples only and does not build individual employment-risk deployment or automated adverse-action workflows.
m7-t2.example: A vendor offers a model that is “90% accurate” at predicting exits. In the company’s synthetic sample, 90% of employees stay. A model that predicts everyone stays would also be 90% accurate while identifying no exits. The analyst must ask better questions.
m7-t2.takeaway: Interpret a simple classifier’s errors and identify why employee-risk predictions require strict governance.

m7-t2.title: Check leakage, drift and authority
m7-t2.summary: Training data must not include information only known after the predicted event, such as an exit-processing date when predicting future exits.
m7-t2.explanation: Training data must not include information only known after the predicted event, such as an exit-processing date when predicting future exits. Evaluate on data not used for training, with appropriate time separation. Performance can drift when roles, policies or populations change. Require authorised purpose, privacy review, fairness assessment, human accountability and a contestability route before any real high-impact use; a vendor accuracy claim is insufficient.
m7-t2.example: In 100 synthetic records, 10 people exit. A model flags 8; 4 of those actually exit. TP=4, FP=4, FN=6 and TN=86. Precision is 4/8=50%, recall 4/10=40%, and accuracy 90/100=90%. The same accuracy as an all-stay baseline conceals very different errors. No metric by itself justifies using the model on real employees.
m7-t2.takeaway: Interpret a simple classifier’s errors and identify why employee-risk predictions require strict governance.

m7-t3.title: A disparity is a signal to investigate
m7-t3.summary: Selection rate is selected eligible applicants divided by eligible applicants under a defined process.
m7-t3.explanation: Selection rate is selected eligible applicants divided by eligible applicants under a defined process. Comparing groups can reveal a disparity worth investigating, but sample size, role mix, job-related criteria and missing data matter. Do not infer demographic attributes from names or photographs. Any real collection or use of sensitive group information requires authorised purpose and safeguards. Classroom groups are synthetic labels, not real identities.
m7-t3.example: A fictional recruitment audit compares two authorised aggregate groups. One has a lower selection rate, but the sample is small and role mix differs. A manager wants to use one ratio either to declare discrimination proven or to declare the process safe. Both conclusions exceed the evidence.
m7-t3.takeaway: Review selection-rate disparities and reporting risks without treating a single ratio as a legal verdict.

items.title: Evidence
items.detail: Calculate both selection rates and the ratio from the fictional group counts.

items.title: Decision
items.detail: Prepare a memo recommending authorised review rather than a legal verdict.

m7-t3.title: Do not turn a heuristic into law
m7-t3.summary: A selection-rate ratio compares one group’s rate with a reference group’s rate.
m7-t3.explanation: A selection-rate ratio compares one group’s rate with a reference group’s rate. The four-fifths heuristic is sometimes discussed in selection auditing, but it is not a universal fairness guarantee or an Indian legal compliance test. A ratio above a chosen screen can still hide harm, and a ratio below it is not by itself a complete legal finding. Escalate substantive concerns to qualified HR and legal reviewers.

m7-t3.title: Govern the proposed action
m7-t3.summary: A responsible review covers purpose, data provenance, affected people, access, disclosure risk, error consequences, alternatives and human accountability.
m7-t3.explanation: A responsible review covers purpose, data provenance, affected people, access, disclosure risk, error consequences, alternatives and human accountability. Consider whether a simpler process improvement answers the need without individual scoring. Provide a way to correct inaccurate data and contest consequential decisions under applicable policy. Document residual limitations and a review date. Technical performance is only one part of a defensible use case.
m7-t3.example: Group A has 20 selections from 50 eligible applicants, a 40% rate. Group B has 12 from 40, a 30% rate. B/A is 0.30/0.40 = 0.75. This flags a difference for careful investigation; it does not establish the reason, legality or correct remedy. Compare like roles, inspect selection stages and review sample limitations using authorised aggregate data.
m7-t3.takeaway: Review selection-rate disparities and reporting risks without treating a single ratio as a legal verdict.
